title: Chia Seed Kheer: A Vegan Janmashtami Dessert That Takes Ten Minutes
excerpt: This no-cook pudding swaps dairy for coconut milk and adds saffron and cardamom for a festive Indian twist on the superfood staple.
body:
• Chia seed kheer combines the protein-and-fiber punch of chia seeds with the festive flavors of cardamom and saffron in a no-cook, vegan dessert
  • The recipe uses just six pantry-friendly ingredients and takes under ten minutes of hands-on time, with the fridge doing the rest overnight
  • Chia seeds deliver omega-3 fatty acids, calcium, and antioxidants, making this a guilt-free alternative to traditional mithai during Janmashtami fasting

Janmashtami calls for sweets, but it does not call for a sugar coma. This chia seed kheer, inspired by the traditional Indian pudding, is vegan, requires no cooking, and can be assembled in under ten minutes. The fridge does the heavy lifting overnight, and you wake up to a creamy, saffron-scented dessert that sits comfortably alongside the panjiri and makhana on the festival spread.

What Makes Chia Kheer Different

Traditional kheer simmers milk and rice for the better part of an hour. Chia kheer skips the stove entirely. Chia seeds absorb roughly 12 times their weight in liquid, forming a thick, pudding-like texture without heat. Swap in coconut milk for dairy, add a pinch of cardamom and a few saffron strands, and the result tastes distinctly Indian without any of the lactose.

"Swap in coconut milk for dairy, add a pinch of cardamom and a few saffron strands, and the result tastes distinctly Indian without any of the lactose."

Chia seeds are nutritional workhorses. A two-tablespoon serving delivers about 4 grams of protein, 11 grams of fiber, and a meaningful dose of omega-3 fatty acids, calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus. For those observing Janmashtami fasting traditions, this makes for a filling, nutrient-dense option that keeps energy steady through the day.

Recipe: Chia Seed Kheer

Ingredients

  • 2 cups coconut milk (from carton, not canned)
  • 6 tablespoons chia seeds
  • 2–4 tablespoons maple syrup or date paste
  • 10–15 saffron strands, soaked in 2 tablespoons warm coconut milk
  • 1 pinch ground cardamom
  • Toppings: chopped pistachios, almonds, coconut flakes, and fresh fruit

Steps

  1. Soak the saffron strands in 2 tablespoons of warm coconut milk and set aside for 5 minutes until the milk turns golden.
  2. In a bowl, combine the remaining coconut milk, chia seeds, maple syrup or date paste, cardamom, and the saffron-milk mixture. Stir well.
  3. Let the mixture sit for 5 minutes, then stir again to break up any clumps of chia seeds.
  4. Cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, or overnight for the best texture.
  5. Before serving, stir the pudding and adjust sweetness if needed. Spoon into small bowls or glasses.
  6. Garnish with chopped pistachios, slivered almonds, coconut flakes, and fresh fruit such as mango or pomegranate seeds.

Tips for a Better Kheer

For a richer texture, substitute half the coconut milk with canned full-fat coconut cream. If you prefer a thinner consistency, add a splash of almond or oat milk after the pudding sets. Date paste gives a deeper, more caramel-like sweetness than maple syrup, and it pairs particularly well with cardamom.

For those following specific Janmashtami fasting rules that exclude certain grains or ingredients, chia seeds are widely accepted as a fasting-friendly food. However, practices vary by family and region, so adjust accordingly.

Why Chia Seeds Deserve a Spot on the Festival Table

The tiny black seeds, originally cultivated by the Aztecs, have become a pantry staple across Indian households in recent years. Beyond their nutritional profile, chia seeds offer a practical advantage for busy festival prep: the pudding can be made the night before and served straight from the fridge, freeing up morning time for puja preparations.

Pair it with a drizzle of rose syrup or a scattering of edible rose petals for a presentation that holds its own against traditional mithai. It is light enough to eat during a fast and satisfying enough to serve as dessert after a full Janmashtami meal.
